catalog_quote: [2.2. Tones] Syllables may bear either a rising or falling tone. The acute accent indicates a rising tone, falling tone is unmarked, e.g. pə́n 'store' and pən 'back'. Minimal pairs in (11) illustrate the contrast between the two tones. The words in column one have a falling-falling (F-F) tone pattern, while words in column two have a falling-rising (F-R) tone pattern. ... kidim 'which is full' kidím 'local doctor' ... tubul 'dew' tubúl 'frog' ... [p.32] In other cases variation between the allomorphs is attested, as in kidil~kədíl 'small'. The [kə] variant is probably a result of destressing the prefix syllable. ... [p.34] However, again presumably in unstressed syllables, the form [tə-] occurs with roots with either back or front vowels. ... [p.99, sec. 5] We note a few aspects of Lamkang grammar that require further investigation: ... 8. Tones, voice quality and stress.

sources.citation: Chelliah, Shobhana L. & Tyler P. Utt. 2017. The syntax and semantics of spatial reference in Lamkang verbs. Himalayan Linguistics 16(1): 28-40. doi:10.5070/H916130760.
sources.quote: 'Lamkang is a tone language, as illustrated by the minimal pair [bu55] 'rice' with high level tone, versus [bu21] 'nest' with low falling tone. There is limited segmental morphophonemics but unusual phonotactics because of C(ə)CV(C) sesquisyllables ... created through productive prefixation, as in kbuu then [kəbu55 tʰen55] 'my share of rice'.' No stress statement.

sources.citation: Chelliah, Shobhana, Rachel Garton, Sumshot Khular & Rex Rengpu Khullar. 2023. Orthography development for languages of the South Central branch of Tibeto-Burman: Lessons from Lamkang. Himalayan Linguistics 22(1): 65-94. doi:10.5070/H922153530.
sources.quote: p.76: 'Tone is phonemic in Lamkang and native speakers can list minimal pairs without much difficulty: e.g., [bu55] 'rice' with high level tone, versus [bu21] 'nest' with low falling tone (Chelliah and Utt 2017). There are also complex tone sandhi rules which are yet to be described.' p.80: 'The preverbal directionals carry stress and prosodically chunk as if they are independent constituents.' (a remark on prosodic wordhood of directionals, not a word-stress rule).
sources.note: Most recent project statement: tone phonemic, 'tone sandhi rules.. yet to be described', preverbal directionals 'carry stress' as independent prosodic chunks; documents that no stress/prosody description has superseded the 2007 sketch.

sources.citation: Burke, Mary, Shobhana Chelliah & Melissa Robinson. 2019. Excrescent vowels in Lamkang prefix sequences. Journal of South Asian Languages and Linguistics 6(2): 185-213. doi:10.1515/jsall-2019-2012 (UNT open postprint via the Internet Archive).
sources.quote: p.188: 'We observe two contrastive tones: falling [mʊl43] 'mountain', and high-level [mʊl44] 'fur'. Prefixes, suffixes, auxiliaries, and clitics may be unspecified for tone. ... After verb stems, we observe regressive tone dissimilation, e.g. if the tone on the suffix is high-level, the tone of the stem will be falling.' pp.185-186: the excrescent prefix vowel 'is unstressed and has the phonetic effect of helping to transition between consonants.' p.207: 'Sesquisyllables are unstressed and reduced ... Lamkang does have some verb stems with complex onsets ... which ... fit the definition of ses
sources.locator: sec. 2, p.188 (tone); abstract/sec. 1 pp.185-186 and sec. 5 p.207 (unstressed excrescent prefix vowels, sesquisyllables)
sources.note: Only instrumental/phonological study of Lamkang after the 2007 sketch; gives the current tone analysis (falling 43 vs high-level 44, toneless affixes, regressive dissimilation) and grounds the record's 'destressed prefix' remark in measured excrescent vowels; should be added to the record's sources as corroboration.
